newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN CRUDE - CHINESE BUYING SOUGHT FOR SEPTEMBER.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN CRUDE - CHINESE BUYING SOUGHT FOR SEPTEMBER.

text.p: Asia's heavy crude market was steady with traders seeking direction from China for the September market, traders said on Friday.
"August trading is almost done, but the September market will depend on whether the Chinese come out" said a trader with a major oil company.
There was still a small volume of Minas and other heavy crudes still available for August, but traders expected these to find buyers without being forced to roll over into September.
But the direction of prices in September was uncertain, with Minas sellers holding out for strong premiums of ICP +60 cents per barrel on expectations of improved demand.
Buyers, meanwhile, were looking at much lower levels, citing the last August Minas trades around ICP +15/25 cents.
Malaysia issued a tender to sell its second cargo of Bunga Kekwa crude, loading in September.
The last tender awarded the first cargo of the medium sweet crude to British Petroleum at Tapis -$1.00.
A September Tapis cargo was sold by Malaysia at Tapis APPI +18/20 cents per barrel.
Despite a firmer light crude market, traders still considered the deal level high, and were surprised that thee was a buyer willing to pay that level.
There was some speculation that the buyer was a Korean trading company who currently buys Tapis from Malaysia on term, and that the cargo was actually a term cargo rather than spot.
But this could not be confirmed.
Malaysia has around 300,000 barrels of Tapis available for September, which had been rolled over from August.
Malaysia said that a U.S. major was showing interest in these barrels for their refinery in Singapore, but no price indication heard.
Trading on the Middle East market remained lacklustre, although traders expected the last few cargoes of Abu Dhabi crudes to be committed very soon.
"They will probably be sold by today, otherwise they'll be rolled into September" said a trader with a major oil company.
"But the volumes are quite small anyway" he added.
Four cargoes of Masila were still available in September, offered by two western traders and a Japanese trading house.
But these were not weighing down the market, with demand heard from China and a US major.
